SPEKANA

I built SPEKANA to turn the pitches I hear in complex textures into material I can compose with. The plugin analyzes live audio from a DAW, displays the spectrum and its most prominent peaks, and lets me capture those peaks as a chord.

From audio to notation

I implemented the analysis in C++ and JUCE using a 2,048-sample Hann window and a 512-sample hop. The detector ranks local peaks by how far they rise above the estimated spectral envelope. The optional Bass Boost mode uses a zero-padded analysis and looks for harmonic support to help surface low fundamentals.

The spectrogram keeps moving while Freeze captures individual chords. The plugin displays the captures on a grand staff and can send them as live MIDI or export them as a MIDI file. In quarter-tone mode, pitch bends on separate MIDI channels let compatible instruments play notes a quarter tone apart.

How I tested it

I used DAW-generated sine tones with known frequencies to check the reported pitches, then tested closely spaced tones to see how the detector separated adjacent peaks. I also used white noise to check what it reported on broadband input. On dense recordings, the peaks are useful as material for composition, and some can be partials or noise rather than played notes.

Accepted for online poster presentation at Audio Developer Conference (ADC Bristol 2026).
